# Brahma Sutra Bhashya | [Adhyaya 3, Pada 3, Adhikarana 7, Sutra 14

For it is indeed the Supreme Being that is taught as higher than all of these; therefore, it is reasonable that the superiority of each one is not being established. Why? Because there is no purpose. For no purpose is seen or heard if superiority is established in the others. However, when the Purusha <note>original: "पुरुष" <gloss>the Self or Supreme Person</gloss></note> is understood as higher than the senses and the rest, and as surpassing all objects, a purpose is seen, namely, the attainment of liberation. And so the Shruti <note>original: "श्रुति" <gloss>scriptural revelation</gloss></note> says: "Having perceived Him, one is liberated from the mouth of death" (Katha Upanishad 3.15). Furthermore, by showing regard for the subject of the Purusha through the negation of the others and through the word *kashtha* <gloss>limit or culmination</gloss>, it indicates that the entire progression from the earlier to the later is for the sake of the realization of the Purusha. This is meant for *akhyana* <gloss>narrative or instruction</gloss>. The meaning is that the narrative exists for the sake of right knowledge. For this narrative is taught solely for the sake of right knowledge, and not that the narrative itself is the primary object. 14

**Due to the word *Atman* also. 15**

From this also it is evident that the statement of the progression of the senses and the rest is solely for the realization of the Purusha. For the reason that it says "This *Atman* <gloss>Self</gloss> hidden in all beings does not shine forth; but it is seen by the subtle, sharp intellect of those who see the subtle" (Katha Upanishad 3.12), it calls the Purusha under discussion the *Atman*. Thus, it is understood that the quality of being the *Atman* is intended to be excluded in the others. It also shows that the Purusha is difficult to know and to be realized by those whose minds are refined. It provides the narrative "The wise man should restrain his speech in the mind" (Katha Upanishad 3.13) for the sake of knowing Him. That has been explained in the section "Even that which is inferred by some" (Brahma Sutra 1.4.1). In this way, of many types—

**Bhamati**

...the limit of something—the Veda, by the indicator of negation of the others and by the indicator of it being the basis of all beings, shows that the purport is in the Purusha. Therefore, it indicates that the statement of superiority of the later over the earlier is for that purpose, he says "Furthermore." He links the Sutra to the fact that because there is no purpose in the others, and the sequence of superiority is for the sake of the realization of the Purusha, thus the narrative is for the sake of instruction. 14. "Due to the word Atman also": Furthermore, because there is uniformity in the opening and the conclusion, such as "That is the supreme step of Vishnu" and "There is nothing higher than the Purusha," upon establishing a unity of meaning focused on the one Purusha, it is not reasonable to assume a difference in sentences or a difference in results, as it would be unnecessarily complex, he says "Furthermore." 15

**Nyaya Nirnaya**

Why? Because the purport is not established regarding the fruitlessness of the others. He thinks, since there is no such fruit, it is not established, and says "Because there is no purpose." How can there be an assertion of a lack of purpose? He considers the alternative of whether the result is established by logic or by scripture, and says "Not so." He replies to the second: "It is also heard." Since the context is seen to be focused on the reality, it cannot be for the sake of a command for meditation. If it is focused on the highest human goal, the knowledge of the truth, then the explanation is possible. The purpose is not to establish the superiority of each one, as that would contradict the logic of the senses and the established doctrine of the human goal. The realization of the superiority of the Purusha is not fruitless. If it were fruitless, one would have to infer the fruit based on the text. Why should the Purusha be the goal if there is no other purpose? He says "However, for the Purusha," because he is the limitless object characterized by being free from all worldly concepts; thus, the absence of destruction is a matter of experience. He sees that for one who has destroyed ignorance and false knowledge, the fruit is seen, so it is not reasonable to imagine an unseen result, and says "It is seen." Regarding the doubt of the wise experience, he cites the Shruti for the result of the vision of the superiority of the Purusha: "And so." From this, because the entire context has this as its purport, he says "Furthermore." The negation "higher than Purusha" is an indicator of the limit, and the word *kashtha* is the boundary; thus, the Veda shows regard for the Purusha. The statement of the progression from the earlier to the later is the statement of the superiority of the later over the earlier. Since there is no command for meditation here, how can the knowledge of the supreme Purusha be for the sake of meditation? He raises this doubt and explains the part of the Sutra: "For the sake of narrative." Even the realization of the attributeless Brahman is for the sake of meditation because it is the state of Brahman. He points to the objection of contradiction with the Shruti "From that, Him..." and says "Right knowledge." 14. He gives another reason why the Purusha alone is to be established here as superior: "Due to the word Atman." He explains the word *cha* <gloss>and</gloss> in the Sutra: "From this also." Clarifying that, he analyzes the word *Atman*: "That which." He wards off the doubt that the non-shining of the Atman is natural: "But it is seen." He says it is "under discussion" because the Atman quality is in that very Shruti. He explains the intended meaning of the words in the Sutra: "Thus also." He performs the task of establishing the remaining meaning: "Of Him." He states the purport of the latter part: "Refined." He states the other reason indicated by the word *cha*: "That." He objects that only the restraint of speech and mind is apparent in the mantra, not a command for meditation: "That has been explained." The meaning is that since the Atman is difficult to know by scripture itself, and the rest are easy to understand, the statement of their superiority is also intended as the primary focus. In this way, the excess of the opening and the conclusion.

<summary>This page continues the commentary on the Brahma Sutras, specifically regarding the Katha Upanishad, arguing that the hierarchical progression of entities (senses, mind, intellect, etc.) is meant to lead the seeker to realize the Supreme Purusha (Atman) rather than to establish the individual superiority of each lower element.</summary>
